lead: An operating system (OS) is the software that sits between applications and hardware. It turns a bare machine into one that is convenient, efficient and safe to share. It manages the CPU, memory, storage and input/output devices, and gives programs clean abstractions such as processes, files and pipes. Every UPI payment, browser tab and IRCTC booking depends on it. This chapter explains what an OS is for, what resources it manages, and how the hardware-software interface is organised.

sections.h3: The OS as manager and virtual machine

blocks.text: An operating system (OS) is software that controls a computer's hardware and provides services to programs. The kernel is the core part that runs with full privilege. A graphical user interface (GUI) is only one program that asks the kernel for work; the OS is not the GUI.

The OS has two jobs. As a resource manager it decides which job gets the central processing unit (CPU), which memory stays in main memory (RAM), and which disk request goes first. As an abstraction layer it hides hardware details: a program writes bytes to a file instead of programming flash blocks. Some syllabi call this the role of the OS, or describe the OS as a virtual machine that gives each program a clean private computer.

Three goals guide the design. Convenience means a programmer need not know disk geometry to save a photo. Efficiency means the CPU and devices should not sit idle when work waits. Ability to evolve means new hardware can be supported without rewriting every app. Fairness and security cut across all three: no app should starve, and one app must not read another's memory.

sections.h3: Resources and the abstractions they become

blocks.text: The OS manages four broad resources. A process is a running program with its own state. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and threads in one process share memory. An address space is the set of memory addresses a process may use. A file is a named sequence of bytes on storage. A pipe is a one-way byte channel between processes. The table pairs each resource with the abstraction a program sees.

blocks.where: busy time is the seconds the CPU executes user or kernel code; total time is the wall-clock interval in seconds; the result is a percentage. A CPU busy 0.8 s in a 1.0 s interval is 80% utilised.

blocks.text: RAM loses data on power loss; disk and flash keep it. The OS moves data between them. Unit 4 covers virtual memory, paging and swapping; Unit 5 covers files and I/O software.

sections.h3: The hardware-software interface and the ISA

blocks.text: The system stack has layers: applications, libraries, the system call interface, the kernel, and hardware. A program calls a library function; the library enters the kernel through a system call; the kernel programs the device. The figure after Section 1 shows this path. The instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between hardware and software. It defines the instructions a CPU can execute, registers, addressing modes, privilege levels, and how traps and interrupts work. A binary compiled for x86-64 does not run directly on an ARM phone. The OS is compiled for an ISA and for the machine's devices.

Device registers often appear as memory addresses, so the kernel uses load and store instructions to control a device. A device raises an interrupt to force the CPU into kernel code; Chapter 1.2 covers buses and interrupts. The mode bit and timer in Chapter 1.4 protect the boundary. Chapter 1.6 covers system call mechanics. Chapter 1.5 lists the services this stack provides. This hardware-software view is part of computer-system organization.

items: An app is written once per API, not once per disk model.
The kernel can change a device driver without changing apps.
A fault in one app can be contained by the kernel.

examples.question: A phone has 8 GB RAM and 8 CPU cores. Four apps each ask for 2.5 GB of data to stay in RAM at the same time. (a) Can all four keep their data in RAM at once? (b) What is the shortfall? (c) How many apps can be fully resident if each needs 2.5 GB? (d) State the OS role in deciding.
steps: Total demanded RAM = 4 apps × 2.5 GB/app = 10.0 GB.
Available RAM = 8 GB. Compare: 10.0 GB > 8 GB, so all four cannot keep their data resident at once.
With 2.5 GB per app, floor(8 GB ÷ 2.5 GB/app) = floor(3.2) = 3 apps fit fully; they use 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 GB and leave 0.5 GB.

The 8 CPU cores can run four apps in parallel, but cores do not add RAM. The OS must keep 3 resident and swap (move some data to storage) or deny the fourth, or reclaim cached memory; Unit 4 covers virtual memory.
Fairness: the OS uses a policy so one app cannot hold RAM forever. Security: it keeps each app's address space separate.
examples.answer: No; demand is 10.0 GB against 8 GB, a 2.0 GB shortfall, so at most 3 apps of 2.5 GB can be fully resident, and the OS must swap, deny or reclaim memory for the fourth.
examples.check:
ram_gb = 8.0
per_app_gb = 2.5
apps = 4
demand_gb = apps * per_app_gb
shortfall_gb = demand_gb - ram_gb
resident_apps = int(ram_gb // per_app_gb)
print(f"{demand_gb:.1f}")
print(f"{shortfall_gb:.1f}")
print(resident_apps)

traps: The OS is not the GUI and not one app; the kernel is only the core part of the OS.
RAM size and CPU core count are different resources. More cores do not add memory; four parallel apps can still run out of RAM.
A process is not a thread. A process owns an address space; threads inside it share that space.
The ISA is not the OS. Linux and Windows on the same ISA are different operating systems.
Virtual memory is not extra RAM. It uses storage to extend the address space, and it can be slower.

quiz.a: An OS controls hardware and provides services to programs. The kernel is the core privileged part that always runs.

quiz.q: Why is the OS not the same as its GUI?
quiz.a: The GUI is one program that asks the kernel for work. The kernel continues when the GUI stops or crashes.

quiz.q: Explain resource manager and abstraction layer with one example each.
quiz.a: As manager, the OS decides which thread gets the CPU and which process gets memory. As abstraction, it gives a file instead of raw disk blocks.

quiz.q: State the three goals of an OS and one challenge that cuts across them.
quiz.a: Convenience, efficiency and ability to evolve. Fairness and security cut across them: no app should starve, and apps must be isolated.

quiz.q: A laptop has 16 GB RAM. Three programs each need 5.5 GB resident. Can all three fit? Give total demand, shortfall and maximum fully resident programs.
quiz.a: Total = 3 × 5.5 = 16.5 GB. Shortfall = 16.5 − 16 = 0.5 GB. Max fully resident = floor(16 ÷ 5.5) = 2 programs, using 11.0 GB; the third must swap or be denied.

quiz.q: Four apps each need 2.5 GB, RAM is 8 GB and there are 8 cores. Which resource is the bottleneck? Does an idle app change the answer? What if the OS overcommits memory?
quiz.a: RAM is the bottleneck: demand is 10.0 GB against 8 GB. An idle app may release pages and free RAM. Overcommit uses virtual memory and can cause thrashing if storage is slow.

quiz.q: Why does hiding disk blocks behind files help hardware evolve? Give one risk.
quiz.a: Apps use a stable file API while drivers and devices change underneath. The risk is a leaky abstraction: some performance effects still reach the app, and a bad driver can hurt the system.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems add containers and hypervisors above or below the kernel, so the same stack appears at several levels. Unikernels and microkernels revisit the size of the privileged core, and eBPF lets safe programs run inside the Linux kernel.
